Hematology.question: ১) What is the value of MCH?
Hematology.exp:
MCH (Mean Corpuscular Hemoglobin) is the average amount of hemoglobin present in one red blood cell. Its normal value is approximately 27–32 picograms (pg) per cell. MCH is calculated as the hemoglobin concentration divided by the red blood cell count. A reduced MCH is commonly seen in hypochromic microcytic anemia, particularly iron deficiency anemia, while an increased MCH may occur in macrocytic anemia. The other options represent different parameters: 76–96 fL corresponds to MCV, 31–35 g/dL corresponds to MCHC, and 6.7–7.7 nm is not a standard red-cell index.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • MCH → 27–32 pg

  • MCV → approximately 80–100 fL

  • MCHC → approximately 32–36 g/dL

  • MCH reflects the hemoglobin content per RBC

  • Low MCH → often hypochromia

Exam Pearl:
MCH = average hemoglobin per RBC, measured in picograms (pg).

Hematology.question: ২) Myeloproliferative disorder excludes....?
Hematology.exp:
Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) is a lymphoproliferative neoplasm, not a myeloproliferative neoplasm (MPN). Classical myeloproliferative neoplasms arise from clonal proliferation of myeloid lineage cells and include polycythemia vera, essential thrombocythemia, and primary myelofibrosis. These disorders are commonly associated with driver mutations such as JAK2, CALR, or MPL. CLL, in contrast, is a malignancy of mature B lymphocytes and belongs to the chronic lymphoid leukemias/lymphoproliferative neoplasms.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Polycythemia vera → MPN

  • Essential thrombocythemia → MPN

  • Primary myelofibrosis → MPN

  • CLL → Lymphoproliferative neoplasm

  • Major MPN driver mutations → JAK2, CALR, MPL

Exam Pearl:
PV + ET + primary myelofibrosis = classic MPNs; CLL is a lymphoid neoplasm.

Hematology.question: ৩) Poikilocytosis means marked variation in.... of RBC?
Hematology.exp:
Poikilocytosis means a variation in the shape of red blood cells (RBCs). It refers to the presence of abnormally shaped RBCs in the peripheral blood film, such as spherocytes, target cells, teardrop cells, sickle cells, and elliptocytes. In contrast, anisocytosis means variation in RBC size, while variation in staining is termed anisocromia. The term “configuration” is not the standard hematological definition used for RBC variation. Poikilocytosis can be seen in various anemias and hematological disorders, particularly severe anemia and disorders affecting erythropoiesis.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Poikilocytosis → variation in RBC shape

  • Anisocytosis → variation in RBC size

  • Anisocromia → variation in RBC staining/color

  • Examples of poikilocytes → spherocytes, target cells, teardrop cells, sickle cells

Exam Pearl:
Poikilocytosis = abnormal variation in RBC shape; anisocytosis = variation in RBC size.

Hematology.question: ৪) Which disorder is not associated with paraproteinemia?
Hematology.exp:
Paraproteinemia refers to the presence of an abnormal monoclonal immunoglobulin (M-protein) produced by a clonal population of plasma cells or B lymphocytes. It is classically associated with multiple myeloma, where malignant plasma cells produce monoclonal immunoglobulins or light chains. Primary (AL) amyloidosis commonly results from deposition of monoclonal immunoglobulin light chains produced by an underlying plasma-cell clone. Some non-Hodgkin lymphomas, particularly lymphoplasmacytic disorders, can also produce paraproteins. CML, however, is a myeloproliferative neoplasm driven by the BCR-ABL1 fusion and is not characteristically associated with paraproteinemia.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Multiple myeloma → M-protein/paraprotein common

  • AL amyloidosis → monoclonal light chains

  • Some NHLs → may produce monoclonal immunoglobulins

  • CML → BCR-ABL1 positive myeloproliferative neoplasm

  • Paraproteinemia → think plasma-cell/B-cell disorders

Exam Pearl:
Paraproteinemia points toward plasma-cell or lymphoplasmacytic disorders; CML is the exception here.

Hematology.question: ৫) Pencil cells are found in.....?
Hematology.exp:
Pencil cells (elliptocytes) are classically associated with iron deficiency anemia (IDA). They are elongated, cigar- or pencil-shaped red blood cells resulting from abnormal erythropoiesis and altered red-cell membrane properties. They are particularly characteristic when iron deficiency is significant. Iron deficiency anemia typically shows microcytosis, hypochromia, increased RDW, and anisopoikilocytosis on the peripheral blood film. Pencil cells can occur in other conditions, but their classic examination association is with iron deficiency anemia. Sickle cell anemia is characterized by sickle cells, while megaloblastic anemia typically shows macro-ovalocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Pencil cells → Iron deficiency anemia

  • IDA → microcytic, hypochromic anemia

  • Peripheral smear → anisopoikilocytosis, pencil cells

  • Sickle cell anemia → sickle cells

  • Megaloblastic anemia → macro-ovalocytes + hypersegmented neutrophils

Exam Pearl:
Pencil cells = Iron deficiency anemia.

Hematology.question: ৬) Which is not a cause of acute DIC?
Hematology.exp:
The question is somewhat ambiguous, because acute leukemia can cause DIC, particularly acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL), which has a strong association with disseminated intravascular coagulation. However, in many traditional exam classifications, acute leukemia in general is not listed as a common cause of acute DIC, whereas obstetrical complications, acute hemolytic transfusion reactions, and septicemia are well-established triggers. Obstetric causes include placental abruption, amniotic fluid embolism, and retained dead fetus. Severe infection, especially sepsis, is a major cause of DIC.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Major acute DIC causes:

    • Sepsis

    • Obstetric complications

    • Acute hemolytic transfusion reaction

    • Major trauma

    • Malignancy, especially APL

  • APL (AML-M3) → particularly associated with DIC.

  • DIC → widespread coagulation activation → consumption of platelets and clotting factors.

Exam Pearl:
For this traditional MCQ, acute leukemia is the intended answer, but remember: APL is a classic cause of DIC.

Hematology.question: ৭) What is the DC of eosinophil?
Hematology.exp:
Eosinophils normally constitute approximately 1–6% of circulating white blood cells in the differential leukocyte count (DLC). They are granulocytes involved mainly in parasitic infections and allergic/hypersensitivity reactions. Eosinophilia is commonly seen in helminthic infections, bronchial asthma, allergic disorders, and some malignancies. The normal differential count for other major leukocytes is approximately: neutrophils 40–75%, lymphocytes 20–40%, monocytes 2–10%, and basophils 0–1%. Therefore, among the given options, 1–6% is the best answer.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Eosinophils → 1–6%

  • Basophils → 0–1%

  • Monocytes → 2–10%

  • Lymphocytes → 20–40%

  • Neutrophils → 40–75%

  • Eosinophilia → think parasites + allergy

Exam Pearl:
Eosinophils normally make up about 1–6% of the total leukocyte count.

Hematology.question: ৮) Hypersegmented neutrophil is found in......?
Hematology.exp:
Hypersegmented neutrophils are a classic peripheral blood film finding in megaloblastic anemia, usually caused by vitamin B12 or folate deficiency. They result from defective DNA synthesis, which causes delayed nuclear maturation in hematopoietic cells while cytoplasmic maturation continues relatively normally. A neutrophil with more than 5 nuclear lobes is generally considered hypersegmented. Megaloblastic anemia also characteristically shows macro-ovalocytes and increased MCV. Iron deficiency anemia produces microcytosis and hypochromia, sickle cell anemia produces sickle-shaped cells, and sideroblastic anemia typically shows microcytic/hypochromic cells with ring sideroblasts in the bone marrow.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Hypersegmented neutrophils → Megaloblastic anemia

  • Common causes → Vitamin B12 and folate deficiency

  • Blood film → Macro-ovalocytes + hypersegmented neutrophils

  • Defect → Impaired DNA synthesis

  • Iron deficiency → Microcytic hypochromic cells

Exam Pearl:
Hypersegmented neutrophils + macro-ovalocytes = megaloblastic anemia.

Hematology.question: ৯) Which stain is commonly used in PBF preparation?
Hematology.exp:
Leishman’s stain is commonly used for preparing and examining a peripheral blood film (PBF), particularly in routine hematology. It is a Romanowsky-type stain containing eosin and methylene blue derivatives, allowing differentiation of RBCs, WBCs, and platelets and assessment of WBC morphology. It is also useful for identifying malarial parasites in blood films. Giemsa is also a Romanowsky stain and is widely used, especially for malaria and hematological morphology, while Wright’s stain is commonly used in many laboratories, particularly in North America. Jenner’s stain is another Romanowsky-type stain but is less commonly used alone for routine PBF examination.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Routine PBF in many MBBS exam settings → Leishman’s stain

  • Giemsa → excellent for malaria and hematoparasites

  • Wright’s → widely used for peripheral blood morphology

  • These belong to the Romanowsky group of stains

Exam Pearl:
For the classic MBBS question “stain commonly used for PBF,” the expected answer is Leishman’s stain.

Hematology.question: ১০) ESR decreases in......?
Hematology.exp:
ESR (erythrocyte sedimentation rate) is usually increased when plasma proteins such as fibrinogen and immunoglobulins promote rouleaux formation. Therefore, ESR is commonly elevated in tuberculosis, multiple myeloma, and inflammatory states. In aplastic anemia, the marked reduction in RBC count can alter sedimentation, but the classic reason for a low ESR is the absence of rouleaux-promoting plasma proteins; importantly, severe anemia itself can actually increase ESR. Among these options, aplastic anemia is the accepted examination answer for decreased ESR. ESR is nonspecific and should not be used alone to diagnose or exclude disease.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • ESR increased in → TB, multiple myeloma, chronic inflammation

  • Increased fibrinogen/immunoglobulins → rouleaux formation → increased ESR

  • ESR may be decreased in → polycythemia, abnormal RBC shapes, severe leukocytosis

  • Aplastic anemia → commonly given as a low-ESR answer in exam questions

Exam Pearl:
For this MCQ, the accepted answer is aplastic anemia; remember that abnormal RBC morphology and polycythemia are classic causes of low ESR.

Hematology.question: ১১) What is the value of BT in ivy's method?
Hematology.exp:
Bleeding time (BT) assesses primary hemostasis, mainly platelet function and platelet–vessel wall interaction. In the Ivy method, the normal bleeding time is approximately 2–6 minutes. A prolonged BT may occur in thrombocytopenia, platelet function disorders, von Willebrand disease, and some vascular disorders. It is generally normal in isolated coagulation factor deficiencies such as hemophilia. The Ivy method uses a blood pressure cuff to maintain standardized venous pressure while a small incision is made on the forearm, and the time until bleeding stops is measured.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Ivy method BT → 2–6 minutes

  • BT assesses → Primary hemostasis

  • Prolonged in → platelet disorders, vWD

  • Hemophilia → BT usually normal

  • PT → extrinsic/common pathway

  • aPTT → intrinsic/common pathway

Exam Pearl:
Ivy bleeding time = 2–6 minutes.

Hematology.question: ১২) Which is abnormal hemoglobin?
Hematology.exp:
HbE (hemoglobin E) is considered an abnormal/variant hemoglobin caused by a mutation in the β-globin gene. It has both structural and mild thalassemic properties and is particularly important in South and Southeast Asian populations. HbA (α₂β₂) is the normal major adult hemoglobin, while HbA₂ (α₂δ₂) and HbF (α₂γ₂) are normal physiological hemoglobin fractions, although their proportions vary with age. HbE is clinically important because HbE/β-thalassemia can produce a significant thalassemia syndrome.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • HbA → normal major adult Hb

  • HbA₂ → normal minor adult Hb

  • HbF → predominant fetal Hb

  • HbE → abnormal hemoglobin variant

  • HbE + β-thalassemia → clinically significant thalassemia

Exam Pearl:
Among the given options, HbE is the abnormal hemoglobin variant.

Hematology.question: ১৩) What is the site of hematopoiesis during postnatal period?
Hematology.exp:
During the postnatal period, the bone marrow is the principal site of hematopoiesis. At birth, hematopoiesis occurs in the marrow of almost all bones. With increasing age, active red marrow becomes progressively restricted to the axial skeleton, including the vertebrae, ribs, sternum, skull, pelvis, and proximal ends of the femur and humerus. The yolk sac is the earliest embryonic site, while the liver becomes the major hematopoietic organ during fetal life, with the spleen contributing as well. In adults, hematopoiesis is normally confined mainly to red bone marrow. Extramedullary hematopoiesis can occur pathologically when marrow function is inadequate.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Earliest embryonic site → Yolk sac

  • Main fetal site → Liver

  • Fetal contribution → Spleen

  • Postnatal/adult main site → Bone marrow

  • Adult active red marrow → mainly axial skeleton

Exam Pearl:
Postnatal hematopoiesis occurs primarily in the bone marrow.

Hematology.question: ১৪) Microcytic anemia excludes.....?
Hematology.exp:
Aplastic anemia is typically a normocytic, normochromic anemia caused by failure of hematopoietic stem cells, leading to pancytopenia and a hypocellular bone marrow. It is therefore not classified as a microcytic anemia. In contrast, iron deficiency anemia, thalassemia, and sideroblastic anemia are classic causes of microcytic hypochromic anemia. Microcytosis results from impaired hemoglobin synthesis, producing smaller-than-normal RBCs. Other important causes of microcytosis include anemia of chronic disease and lead poisoning.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Microcytic anemia → IDA, thalassemia, sideroblastic anemia

  • Other causes → anemia of chronic disease, lead poisoning

  • Aplastic anemia → usually normocytic normochromic

  • Aplastic anemia → pancytopenia + hypocellular marrow

Exam Pearl:
Microcytic anemia = defective hemoglobin synthesis; aplastic anemia is usually normocytic and is the exception here.

Hematology.question: ১৫) Which is used in parenteral iron therapy?
Hematology.exp:
Iron sorbitol is a preparation used for parenteral iron therapy, particularly when oral iron is ineffective, poorly tolerated, or contraindicated. Traditional parenteral iron preparations include iron sorbitol, iron dextran, iron sucrose, and ferric carboxymaltose. In contrast, ferrous sulphate and ferrous fumarate are standard oral iron preparations. Although ferric gluconate is also available as an intravenous iron preparation, the classic answer for this MCQ is iron sorbitol. Parenteral iron is generally reserved for situations such as malabsorption, intolerance to oral iron, or the need for rapid iron replacement.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Iron sorbitol → parenteral iron

  • Ferrous sulphate → oral

  • Ferrous fumarate → oral

  • Modern IV preparations → iron sucrose, ferric carboxymaltose, ferric gluconate

  • Parenteral iron → consider when oral iron is ineffective or not tolerated

Exam Pearl:
Classic exam answer: Iron sorbitol is a parenteral iron preparation.

Hematology.question: ১৬) Which is the final stage of maturation of nucleated cell series?
Hematology.exp:
In the erythroid series, the reticulocyte is the final stage before the mature RBC. However, among the options, orthochromatic erythroblast (normoblast) is the last nucleated erythroid cell. The nucleus is extruded from the orthochromatic erythroblast, forming a reticulocyte, which still contains residual RNA but no nucleus. The reticulocyte then matures into a mature erythrocyte.

Sequence:
Proerythroblast → Basophilic erythroblast → Polychromatic erythroblast → Orthochromatic erythroblast → Reticulocyte → RBC

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Last nucleated erythroid cell → Orthochromatic erythroblast

  • Last immature RBC stage → Reticulocyte

  • Mature RBC → Erythrocyte

Exam Pearl:
If the question asks “final stage of maturation of nucleated cell series”, the answer is orthochromatic erythroblast. If it asks “final stage before mature RBC”, answer reticulocyte.

Hematology.question: ১৭) Hemoglobin electrophoresis is done to diagnose.....?
Hematology.exp:
Hemoglobin electrophoresis separates different hemoglobin types based on their electrical charge and is commonly used to diagnose thalassemia and hemoglobinopathies. In β-thalassemia, electrophoresis typically shows increased HbA₂ and often increased HbF, with reduced HbA in more severe forms. It is also useful for detecting variants such as HbS, HbC, and HbE.

Iron deficiency anemia, sideroblastic anemia, and aplastic anemia are not primarily diagnosed by hemoglobin electrophoresis; they are evaluated using CBC, peripheral blood film, iron studies, and, when appropriate, bone marrow examination.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Hb electrophoresis → Thalassemia & hemoglobinopathies

  • β-thalassemia trait → ↑ HbA₂

  • β-thalassemia major → ↑ HbF, markedly ↓/absent HbA

  • HbS/HbE → detected by electrophoresis

Exam Pearl:
Suspect a hemoglobinopathy → think hemoglobin electrophoresis.

Hematology.question: ১৮) Infusion of 1 unit of blood causes...... increment of Hb level?
Hematology.exp:
In an average adult, transfusion of 1 unit (approximately 1 unit of packed RBCs) raises the hemoglobin level by about 1 g/dL. The exact increment depends on the patient’s blood volume, ongoing bleeding, and the type/volume of blood product transfused.

For packed red blood cells (PRBCs), the standard exam rule is:
1 unit PRBC → Hb ↑ ≈ 1 g/dL and Hct ↑ ≈ 3% in a typical adult.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • 1 unit PRBC → Hb ↑ ~1 g/dL

  • 1 unit PRBC → Hct ↑ ~3%

  • Ongoing bleeding → expected rise may be less

Exam Pearl:
“One unit PRBC = approximately +1 g/dL Hb.”

Hematology.question: ১৯) Which is not true about reticulocytes?
Hematology.exp:
Reticulocytes are immature red blood cells that have already extruded their nucleus but still contain residual ribosomal RNA, giving them a reticulated appearance with special stains. They are biconcave, disc-shaped, and non-nucleated. However, reticulocytes are slightly larger than mature RBCs, not smaller. As they mature, they lose residual RNA and decrease slightly in size to become mature erythrocytes.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Reticulocyte → Non-nucleated

  • Shape → Biconcave disc

  • Size → Slightly larger than mature RBC

  • Contains residual RNA

  • Normal reticulocyte count → approximately 0.5–2.5%

Exam Pearl:
Reticulocytes are slightly larger than mature RBCs—so “slightly smaller” is NOT true.

Hematology.question: ২০) Which is not true about AML?
Hematology.exp:
Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is predominantly a disease of adults, and diagnosis typically involves increased myeloblasts in the peripheral blood and/or bone marrow. AML generally has a poorer prognosis than ALL in adults, although prognosis varies considerably by cytogenetic and molecular subtype.

Lymphadenopathy is not a typical prominent feature of AML. It is much more commonly associated with ALL and some lymphoid malignancies. AML may occasionally cause lymph node enlargement, but it is not considered a classical feature.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • AML → predominantly adults

  • Myeloblasts in blood/bone marrow

  • Auer rods → strongly support myeloid differentiation

  • Lymphadenopathy → more typical of ALL

  • AML → generally poor prognosis, depending on subtype

Exam Pearl:
AML = adult + myeloblast + Auer rods; prominent lymphadenopathy favors ALL.

Hematology.question: ২১) Classical hemolytic uremic syndrome excludes.....?
Hematology.exp:
Classical hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS) is characterized by the classic triad of:

  1. Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia

  2. Thrombocytopenia

  3. Acute kidney injury (AKI/ARF)

It commonly follows a diarrheal illness caused by Shiga toxin–producing E. coli. Peripheral blood film may show schistocytes (red cell fragments). Neutrophilia can occur as a nonspecific response to infection or inflammation, but it is not one of the classical defining features of HUS.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • HUS triad → Hemolytic anemia + thrombocytopenia + AKI

  • Common cause → Shiga toxin–producing E. coli

  • PBF → Schistocytes

  • Related condition → TTP

  • HUS → renal involvement is prominent

Exam Pearl:
HUS = MAHA + thrombocytopenia + acute renal failure; neutrophilia is not part of the classical triad.

Hematology.question: ২২) Features of ITP excludes.....?
Hematology.exp:
Immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) is an acquired autoimmune disorder characterized by isolated thrombocytopenia due to increased platelet destruction, mainly in the spleen. Typical manifestations include petechiae, purpura, and mucosal bleeding. Bone marrow examination, when performed, may show increased megakaryocytes due to compensatory platelet production. Hepatosplenomegaly is not a typical feature of ITP; significant hepatosplenomegaly should prompt consideration of another diagnosis such as leukemia, lymphoma, or hypersplenism.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • ITP → isolated thrombocytopenia

  • Bleeding → petechiae, purpura, mucosal bleeding

  • Bone marrow → ↑ megakaryocytes

  • Usually no hepatosplenomegaly

  • PT/aPTT → generally normal

Exam Pearl:
ITP = isolated thrombocytopenia + increased megakaryocytes + no hepatosplenomegaly.

Hematology.question: ২৩) Which leukemia may involve CNS?
Hematology.exp:
ALL is the leukemia most classically associated with central nervous system (CNS) involvement, particularly in children. Leukemic blasts can infiltrate the meninges, producing headache, vomiting, cranial nerve palsies, seizures, or other neurological features. Because CNS involvement can occur even without symptoms, CNS-directed prophylaxis (e.g., intrathecal chemotherapy) is an important component of ALL treatment.

AML can also involve the CNS, but ALL is the classic exam answer among these options.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • ALL → CNS involvement common/classically tested

  • CNS disease → leukemic meningeal infiltration

  • CNS prophylaxis → intrathecal chemotherapy

  • AML → CNS involvement possible, especially certain subtypes

Exam Pearl:
When asked which leukemia classically involves the CNS → think ALL.

Hematology.question: ২৪) DD of gum bleeding excludes....?
Hematology.exp:
Gum bleeding (gingival bleeding) is commonly seen in disorders causing thrombocytopenia or platelet dysfunction. ITP, leukemia, and aplastic anemia can all cause bleeding manifestations due to reduced platelet count.

Lymphoma is not a typical primary cause of gum bleeding, so it is the best answer as the exception. Although some lymphomas can rarely involve the oral cavity or cause cytopenias, gum bleeding is not a classical presenting feature.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • ITP → thrombocytopenia → petechiae, purpura, gum bleeding

  • Leukemia → thrombocytopenia ± gingival infiltration

  • Aplastic anemia → pancytopenia → bleeding

  • Lymphoma → not a classic cause of gum bleeding

Exam Pearl:
Gum bleeding → think platelet disorders, especially ITP, leukemia, and aplastic anemia; lymphoma is the exception here.

Hematology.question: ২৫) Trephine biopsy usually taken from which site?
Hematology.exp:
A trephine biopsy (bone marrow core biopsy) is usually taken from the posterior iliac crest, specifically the posterior superior iliac spine region. It provides a cylindrical core of bone and marrow, allowing assessment of marrow cellularity, architecture, fibrosis, infiltration, and focal lesions.

The sternum is used for bone marrow aspiration in selected settings, but it is not used for trephine biopsy because of the risk of injury to mediastinal structures. The proximal tibia may be used for marrow access in some pediatric situations, but it is not the routine adult site.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Trephine biopsy → posterior iliac crest

  • Bone marrow aspiration → usually posterior iliac crest

  • Sternum → aspiration only; not trephine biopsy

  • Proximal tibia → possible pediatric site, not routine adult site

Exam Pearl:
Trephine biopsy = posterior iliac crest.
